evals.name: reach-and-enable
evals.prompt: Our team opens http://chronicle.internal:35000/ and fails; later someone sets Features:Api=false to reduce the attack surface and the Workbench vanishes. Explain the correct URL, why, and what happened after the config change. Reply only.
evals.expected_output: Kernel port 35000 is TLS because HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 multiplex through ALPN, so use https://<host>:35000/. Features:Workbench is ANDed with Features:Api; setting Api to false silently disables the Workbench because it is a client of that API. Configuration is under Cratis:Chronicle from chronicle.json or Cratis__Chronicle__ environment variables.
assertions: Says the URL is https://<host>:35000/ because the port is TLS with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 multiplexed through ALPN.
Says Features:Workbench is ANDed with Features:Api so setting Features:Api to false silently disables the Workbench.
Says the Workbench is a client of the HTTP API.
Names the configuration location as Cratis:Chronicle in chronicle.json or Cratis__Chronicle__ environment variables.

evals.name: exposure-decision
evals.prompt: A colleague proposes exposing the Workbench to the office network with Authentication:Enabled=false and says the client route guard protects it anyway, and that the Workbench masks personal data. Assess the claims. Reply only.
evals.expected_output: The static bundle is served anonymously by design; the client-side route guard is a UX affordance, not an access control; authorization is on the API calls. Disabling authentication removes it everywhere: every gRPC and HTTP endpoint answers anonymously, publishing the whole store. The Workbench applies no PII masking or redaction; assume operators see plaintext. Forwarded headers are trusted only from loopback or configured known proxies.
assertions: Says the application bundle is served anonymously and the client-side route guard is not an access control.
Says turning authentication off makes every gRPC service and HTTP endpoint answer anonymously, publishing the whole event store to anyone who can reach it.
Says the Workbench applies no PII masking, field redaction or data classification and operators should be assumed to see plaintext personal data.
Says forwarded headers are trusted only from loopback or configured known proxies by default.

evals.name: no-confirmation-buttons
evals.prompt: Which of these Workbench actions ask for confirmation in the UI and which fire on the first click: Clear quarantine, Retry partition, Stop/Resume/Delete job, Perform recommendation, Replay observer, Remove observer, Ignore recommendation, Redact event? And does a missing dialog imply permission? Reply only.
evals.expected_output: No confirmation: Clear quarantine, Retry partition, Stop/Resume/Delete job, Perform recommendation. Confirmed: Replay observer, Remove observer, Ignore recommendation, Redact (twice: a confirmation and a required reason). A missing confirmation dialog is not permission; decide before clicking. Inspection does not authorize mutation.
assertions: Lists Clear quarantine, Retry partition, Stop/Resume/Delete job and Perform recommendation as firing without a confirmation dialog.
Lists Replay observer, Remove observer, Ignore recommendation and Redact event as confirmed in the UI.
Says Redact requires a confirmation and a required reason.
Says a missing confirmation dialog is not permission and a request to inspect does not authorize a mutation.

evals.name: redact-revise-erasure
evals.prompt: A password was appended in an event. Someone proposes using Revise to fix it, then also using Redact for a GDPR subject erasure request. Explain what Redact and Revise do, what to check before Revise, and whether either answers an erasure request. Reply only.
evals.expected_output: Redact removes event content, retained causation property values, revision history and content hashes; requires a reason; records itself; does not reach backups, oplogs or already-forwarded events. Revise rewrites content; its confirmation lists the observers to be replayed, the blast radius. Neither is the mechanism for personal-data erasure, which is the kernel's key-destruction path keyed by compliance subject. The CLI has no equivalent.
assertions: Says Redact removes event content, retained causation values, revision history and content hashes, requires a reason and does not reach backups, oplogs or already-forwarded events.
Says Revise rewrites event content and that its confirmation lists the observers that will be replayed, which is the blast radius to read before confirming.
Says neither Redact nor Revise is the mechanism for a personal-data erasure request, which is the kernel's key-destruction path by compliance subject.
Says redaction and revision are Workbench-only with no CLI equivalent.

evals.name: reset-and-fast-forward
evals.prompt: An operator wants to use Fast forward on a lagging observer in production and, to start clean, Reset kernel state from Development Tools. Explain what each does and the protection (or lack of it) in production builds. Reply only.
evals.expected_output: Fast forward skips every unhandled event, discards failed partitions and retains already-built state: deliberate loss of pending processing, not a repair or replay. Reset kernel state is the most destructive operation; the operation is compiled in only for development builds (in other builds the gRPC call exists, answers anonymously, and is a no-op), the screen reports unavailable, and a dialog guards it. Never run it against a store whose data is needed; production is protected by the operation not being there, not by authentication.
assertions: Says Fast forward skips every unhandled event, discards failed partitions and retains already-built state, and is not a repair or replay.
Says Reset kernel state is the most destructive operation and must never be run against a store whose data anyone needs.
Says the reset operation is compiled in only for development builds and in other builds the call is a no-op that answers anonymously.
Says production is protected by the operation not being there rather than by authentication.
